---
title: "Count overdispersion"
execute:
  warning: false
  message: false
---

The fitted Nettle model gives us a concrete way to compare the spread it permits with the discrepancies in the observed country counts. We will fit the Poisson mean first, then inspect actual countries whose fitted means lie near the middle of the fitted range.

Recall that [variance](../random-variables-and-distributions/variance-and-covariance.qmd#variance-as-expected-squared-distance) is the expected squared distance from the mean. **Overdispersion** means that the response varies more than the fitted family's variance permits after we condition on the predictors. This definition always refers to a model: a dataset is not overdispersed in isolation.

We diagnose the mismatch with [Pearson residuals](residuals.qmd). A Pearson residual divides the difference between an observed and fitted value by the conditional standard deviation that the model assigns to that row. If the variance model is adequate, the squared standardized discrepancies should have roughly the amount of variation their scale predicts.

The Pearson sum is calibrated using a row [independence](../foundations/independence.qmd) approximation. If known groups share unmodeled information, [fixed and random effects](fixed-and-random-effects.qmd) later provide a model for deviations belonging to each group. We do not need that construction merely to calculate the present diagnostic.

The Pearson ratio can show the size of the mismatch against fitted Poisson means,
but several measurement and stochastic processes can create that mismatch. The
calculation is therefore followed by a statement of what the evidence can and cannot tell us about models rather than an
automatic distribution switch.

```{r}
#| label: load-nettle-dispersion
#| echo: true
nettle <- read.csv("data/nettle/nettle-1999-climate.csv")
fit <- glm(language_count ~ mean_growing_season_months + offset(log_area_km2),
           poisson(), nettle)
nettle$fitted <- fitted(fit)
nettle$pearson <- residuals(fit, type = "pearson")
dispersion <- sum(nettle$pearson^2) / df.residual(fit)
dispersion
```

The following rows are the three observed countries whose fitted means are closest to the median fitted mean. `poisson_sd` is the standard deviation the Poisson model assigns to each row, while `observed_minus_fitted` is the discrepancy in the recorded count.

```{r}
#| label: observed-nettle-spread-example
middle_fit <- median(nettle$fitted)
middle_rows <- order(abs(nettle$fitted - middle_fit))[1:3]
transform(
  nettle[middle_rows, c("country", "language_count", "fitted")],
  poisson_sd = sqrt(fitted),
  observed_minus_fitted = language_count - fitted
)
```

These rows make the scale comparison literal. The full Pearson ratio below then aggregates the squared, standardized discrepancies across all countries rather than relying on a selected example.

The **Pearson dispersion ratio** is

$$
\widehat\phi_P=\frac{1}{n-p}\sum_i
\frac{(y_i-\widehat\lambda_i)^2}{\widehat\lambda_i}.
$$

Recall that the [likelihood](../statistical-inference/maximum-likelihood.qmd)
holds the observed country totals fixed while comparing possible Poisson mean
parameters. In that fitted Poisson likelihood, $\widehat\phi_P$ is a diagnostic
rather than an estimate of a free Poisson parameter: the Poisson variance is
fixed at $\lambda_i$. Under the enlarged quasi-Poisson variance model
$\operatorname{Var}[Y_i\mid x_i]=\phi\lambda_i$, the same ratio estimates the
dispersion multiplier $\phi$.

Under that enlarged model, the ratio is an estimator before the sample is
observed and its realized value is an estimate of $\phi$; see the
[estimators are random variables](../statistical-inference/properties-of-estimators.qmd#estimators-are-random-variables).

The numerator is the sum of squared standardized residuals because a Poisson row has model variance $\widehat\lambda_i$:

$$
r_i^P=\frac{y_i-\widehat\lambda_i}{\sqrt{\widehat\lambda_i}},
\qquad
\sum_i(r_i^P)^2=\sum_i\frac{(y_i-\widehat\lambda_i)^2}{\widehat\lambda_i}.
$$

The denominator $n-p$ accounts approximately for the $p$ fitted mean parameters. Under a correctly specified [independent](../foundations/independence.qmd#why-the-characterizations-are-equivalent) Poisson model, the numerator is approximately chi-squared with $n-p$ degrees of freedom, so the ratio fluctuates around one rather than equaling one exactly.

A Poisson model expects a value near one. The observed value is `r round(dispersion, 2)`, so the conditional variance restriction fails badly for this specification.

```{r}
#| label: plot-nettle-dispersion
#| echo: true
library(ggplot2)
ggplot(nettle, aes(fitted, pearson)) +
  geom_hline(yintercept = 0, color = "grey70", linewidth = .4) +
  geom_point(size = 1.5, color = "#1F5A85") +
  scale_x_log10() +
  labs(x = "Fitted language count", y = "Pearson residual") +
  theme_classic()
```

```{r}
#| label: observed-versus-fitted-count-variance
#| echo: true
nettle$fitted_bin <- cut(nettle$fitted,
  unique(quantile(nettle$fitted, seq(0, 1, length.out = 6))),
  include.lowest = TRUE)
variance_by_bin <- aggregate(cbind(language_count, fitted) ~ fitted_bin, nettle,
  function(z) c(mean = mean(z), variance = var(z), n = length(z)))
variance_by_bin
```

These bins are descriptive. A within-bin observed variance much larger than its fitted mean is compatible with overdispersion, but sparse bins and a changing mean can also produce gaps.

A large Pearson ratio shows that conditional variability exceeds the fitted Poisson
variance. Omitted predictors, dependence, latent heterogeneity, and a different
count family can all produce that result, so the statistic by itself does not
select among those explanations. In this application, country boundaries and
documentation practices may also contribute to the excess variation because they
help determine the recorded count.

| Possible source | Evidence to inspect | Corresponding next model |
|---|---|---|
| Mean formula too coarse | residual trend against climate or area | revise predictors or functional form |
| Unobserved unit heterogeneity | extra variance without a known cluster | negative binomial mixture |
| Known clustered dependence | repeated observations within a group | random effects or clustered uncertainty |
| Mean plausible, variance scaled | coefficient estimates stable but SEs too small | quasi-Poisson uncertainty |
| More zeros than a single count process predicts | zero frequency and process knowledge | hurdle or zero-inflated model |

Here a **random effect** means a deviation for one group represented as a draw
from a shared distribution. That construction, introduced later in [fixed and
random effects](fixed-and-random-effects.qmd), can represent known clusters; it is
not licensed merely by observing a large Pearson ratio.

## Recap and check

1. Does $\widehat\phi=2$ prove a negative binomial data generating process? No. Several failures can inflate the same statistic.
2. Must a correct Poisson fit produce exactly one? No. The statistic has sampling variation around one.

[Quasi-Poisson regression](quasi-poisson.qmd) changes uncertainty while retaining the fitted mean; [negative binomial regression](negative-binomial-regression.qmd) changes the conditional variance model.
